name: Scrotal cooling / ball icing

lead: Scrotal cooling, or 'ball icing', is applying cold to the testes in the hope of supporting testosterone and sperm quality, and through testosterone a leaner, more muscular, more masculine look.

The idea comes from established physiology: the scrotum keeps the testes about two to three degrees Celsius below core body temperature, and heat is known to affect sperm production. Proponents extend that to deliberate extra cooling. No study of deliberate cooling in healthy men for hormones or appearance was found.

paras: Users apply an ice pack, cold pack or cold water to the area for short sessions, usually wrapped in cloth, often as a recurring habit alongside other hormone-focused routines. Nothing in the reviewed material describes a timeline for results.

Direct ice contact can cause skin cold injury. The cremaster muscle pulls the testes upward in cold, and the body already regulates testicular temperature on its own. The effect of extra cooling in healthy men has not been studied.

angle.text: Some men cool the testes with ice or cold packs, aiming to support testicular function, testosterone and the muscle and masculine features that follow. It draws on real testicular heat sensitivity; the practice itself has not been studied for hormones or appearance.

lead: Scrotal cooling, informally 'ball icing', is a fringe practice in which men apply ice, cold packs or cold water to the scrotum, hoping to improve sperm quality or testosterone. It is discussed in biohacking and fertility-optimisation circles and occasionally on looksmaxxing forums.

The looks connection is through testosterone: in looksmaxxing culture, higher testosterone is associated with muscle mass, leanness, facial and body hair and other masculine traits, so anything believed to support testicular function is of interest. Sperm quality is a related fertility concern rather than an appearance one.

The idea builds on documented physiology: the scrotum keeps the testes about two to three degrees Celsius below core body temperature, and higher temperatures affect spermatogenesis.[1][2] A 2013 systematic review found eight articles on scrotal cooling and spermatogenesis and reported insufficient evidence for firm conclusions, with a positive trend toward improved fertility.[3]
infobox: Small fertility studies and device trials

paras: Practitioners describe brief applications of cold to the scrotal area. The rationale offered is that cooler testes mean better sperm production, extending the known effects of heat. Details vary by account.

The scrotum holds the testes at about 35 C, a few degrees below the core temperature of 37 C. The cremaster muscle and the dartos fascia adjust the testes' distance from the body, and the scrotum usually tightens in cold.[1]

Another reference says sperm production is most efficient slightly below core temperature, with efficiency falling both below and above about 33 C, and that temperatures above roughly 36.7 C impede it.[2] In mice, brief scrotal heat stress caused DNA damage, reduced fertility and abnormal embryonic development.[2] A fertility reference reports that sustained high ambient temperature consistently lowers sperm quality in animals and links heat to lower sperm quality in humans.[4]
Leydig cells in the testes produce testosterone under pituitary luteinizing hormone control.[2]

Researchers have developed cooling products for fertility research, including a hydrogel scrotal cooling patch tested in a registered randomised controlled trial protocol of men with low sperm counts, and specialised cooling underwear.[5][6] In a prospective study of cyclic cooling underwear, median scrotal skin temperature was 34.6 C in the cooling period versus 35.3 C in the control period, a reduction of 0.7 C, which the authors described as feasible without impairing daily activities.[6]

A 2013 systematic review of eight articles concluded there was insufficient evidence for firm conclusions on scrotal cooling and male fertility, while observing a positive trend, and called for well designed randomised trials.[3] A 2016 review of lifestyle and complementary therapies for male infertility described the data for scrotal cooling, along with acupuncture and several other therapies, as sparse or inconclusive.[7] A 1982 report described testis hypothermia for infertility due to poor semen.[8]
No studies were found of deliberate home cooling in healthy men for testosterone or appearance.

The sources reviewed do not describe cooling-specific harms in the research devices. General concerns include skin cold injury from direct ice contact. Reference sources also note that the cremasteric reflex raises the testes in response to cold.[2]
